newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Roche says sales strong, profits to rise.
newsitem.headline: Roche says sales strong, profits to rise.

text.p: Pharmaceuticals group Roche Holding AG on Tuesday reported a lower-than-expected 18 percent rise in 1997 first quarter sales, but forecast another rise in full-year profits.
"Barring unforeseen events -- the usual, but necessary rider -- we expect 1997 to produce another good result and an increase in profits," Roche chairman Fritz Gerber told a news conference.
Roche, one of the world's most profitable drug companies, had a 1996 group net profit of 3.90 billion Swiss francs ($2.7 billion), up 16 percent from the 3.37 billion posted for 1995.
Group sales in 1996 rose 10.7 percent to 15.966 billion.
Gerber also said Roche had no plans to diversify and any possible acquisitions would be within its core business areas.
He added Roche had no plans to either split or buy back its shares, a move stock markets have frequently hoped for.

The line of questioning follows months of recurring speculation about whether the Swiss pharmaceuticals group might use a cash hoard estimated at about 15 billion Swiss francs to make a major acquisition or for a partial buyback of its participation certificates.
"We have no plans and would rather use the money for other opportunities that might arise," Gerber said.
In London the shares of Zeneca Group Plc fell as hopes of a bid from Roche faded.
First quarter sales rose to 4.45 billion francs from 3.785 billion in the 1996 first quarter and the growth trend for the major established products and new entries remained unchanged.
Adjusting for fluctuating exchange rates, sales rose three percent in local currency terms. In Swiss franc terms first quarter sales rose 18 percent.
"Worldwide, sales of the division's six top-selling drugs were well up for the period, with Rocephin, Neupogen and Ticlid posting double-digit gains in local currencies," Roche said.
Nevertheless, the market was disappointed by the results.
Roche's non-voting equity securities fell 45 francs, or 0.4 percent, to 11,885 francs and some analysts saw the share putting a damper on the entire Swiss market.
"The mere three percent rise is very disappointing when you consider that sales grew an average 8.5 percent in 1996," one Zurich trader said.
Sales of the group's pharmaceuticals division were three percent higher on a local currency basis and 19 percent higher in Swiss francs.

Roche said local currency sales growth in pharmaceuticals would have exceeded six percent if not for a sharper than expected drop in U.S. first quarter sales of the epilepsy drug Rivotril/Klonopin and analgesia drug Toradol, two products hit by generic competition.
The local currency sales rise was below the expectations of many analysts.
"I was expecting seven percent," said Romain Pasche of Union Bancaire Privee in Geneva.
"This has to be expected due to generics," Pasche said.
However, he said prospects for three new drugs due to come to market this year should more than offset the sales drops for the more mature drugs just mentioned.

Roche executives said their efforts will be focused this year on launching a new cardiovascular agent called Posicor, an anti-obesity product named Xenical and a Parkinson's disease treatment called Tasmar.
"The successful launch of these innovative products will require us to significantly expand our sales organisation serving the general practitioner segment," Roche said.
"We are thus responding to the increasing importance of ambulatory health care delivery."
Early this year advisory panels in the United States and Europe recommended approval of Posicor for treatment of high blood pressure and angina pectoris.
Pasche said the sales target for Posicor is 550 million francs, for Xenical 500 million and for Tasmar 200 million when the products are fully on stream by the year 2002.
Sales of AIDS drug Invirase rose far ahead of the high growth that had been forecast and sales of CellCept, used in kidney transplants, more than doubled in local currencies.
($ = 1.468 Swiss Francs)
